doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Musical chairs, band books and Goodman's bebop band
summary: Players hop bands; Goodman's rewritten bebop book had no 'Sing Sing Sing' but still danceable.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Oh absolutely. But people always think about you you did this, you did that and you played with this band or you played with that band. It’s not like today. Like if you play with Bruce Springsteen, you play with him for life. Those guys never change jobs. We were jumping all over the place all the time. Those guys stay in the same jobs all their lives you know. Why would you leave a job that pays you four thousand million a year?
It literally was musical chairs, wasn’t it.

Oh yeah, sure. I knew guys, great musicians, who would play with the band for two or three months, as soon as they learned the book they wanted to play with another band and learn another book. You know they got tired of playing the same music. You know essentially, you know everyone said oh you’re playing with Woody Herman, you’re playing with Benny Goodman. Sure it’s marvelous, the degree of musicianship is so much higher than the B bands, that sort of thing. But the remuneration isn’t that much higher. It’s the artistic satisfaction you get and like playing, but you do play the same music all the time. Everybody thinks when you play a book — like Woody for instance didn’t care if a drummer could read or not, because he figured if he had an ear in two weeks he could memorize the whole book and there wouldn’t be any problem. He’d just tell you when to lay out if you had to lay out, that sort of thing. Benny Goodman never knew if I could read or not I don’t think but it didn’t make any difference. Because when you were with those bands everybody thinks that well geez you get to play “Four Brothers” every night and you get to play “Don’t Be That Way” every night. And when I was with Benny I never played “Sing Sing Sing.” We didn’t have that in the book. Because he had the book rewritten all in the bebop vein. That was the bebop band that Benny had. And so he had the book rewritten. So we never played “Sing Sing Sing” because that was the old Benny Goodman. He didn’t want to do that at that time. But then he started doing it again when he had his bands after that. But I never got to play that © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
with him and that used to be one of my big numbers in high school man, I used to play that record over and over and over.
Did the people, your audiences, have a harder time dancing to the bebop band of Benny Goodman?

I don’t think so, no. The tempos were still medium dance. It’s kind of the musical structure rather than the basic rhythm. See the basic rhythm was still a good steady four- four so people were dancing. I don’t think Benny would be the type that if he had a drummer that played outside too much he would be comfortable. Because he was a real strong rhythmic player and so he was a marvelous player, geez. Beautiful sense of time and swing. So he knew what he wanted in the band. So esoterically there were people who would say well that’s not really bebop, it’s not doing this, it’s not doing that, it’s not doing this. But it was the structure of the music more, the way the arrangements changed the voicings and some of the brass figures and stuff like that.
